full_judgment:
3. The facts relevant for disposal of the present revisional application, in short, are that the opposite party No. 1 as Pre-emptor filed Pre-emption Case No. 25 of 2005 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (SAT Act) contending, inter alia, that Sreedham Chandra Dhar and Gourangra Chandra Dhar were the owners of the land of Plot No. 37 under SA Khatian No. 4 and they had gifted 62 decimals of land from the said plot by a registered deed dated 30-12-1981 to Suresh Chandra Dhar, the grandfather of the Pre-emptor Suresh Chandra Dhar. Suresh Chandra Dhar died leaving behind Sunil Chandra Dhar and Krisno Chandra Dhar as his legal heirs. Thereafter Sunil Chandra Dhar died leaving behind 03 (three) sons, the Pre-emptor and the opposite party Nos. 4 and 5. Subsequently, Subol Chandra Dhor transferred 19.5 decimals by deed No. 6536 dated 21-7-2005 who is a stranger purchaser without giving any proposal of sale of the land to the Pre-emptor who is a co-sharer in the land. The Pre-emptor came to know about the transfer on 2-10-2005 and after obtaining certified copy of the disputed deed on 5-10-2005 filed the Pre-emption case. 

 4. The Pre-emptee contested the case by filing a written objection denying all the material allegations made in the Pre-emption petition stating further that the case is bad for defect of parties as well as barred by limitation and also barred by waiver, estoppels and acquiescence. It is also stated that the opposite party No. 2 Subol Chandra Dhar obtained the land by way inheritance. The Pre-emptor was given a notice of sale but he refused to purchase the land. Thereafter the Pre-emptee purchased the land by a registered deed dated 21-7-2005 and took possession therein. At the time of taking possession of the land the Pre-emptor was present there. 

 11. It appears from the record that the pre-emptor being petitioner filed Pre-emption Case No. 25 of 2005 before the learned Assistant Judge, Muktagacha, Mymensingh claiming the property for getting the same by way of pre-emption. In the pre-emption petition the pre-emptor did not clearly state that he is a co-sharer by way of inheritance in the case land. The learned Assistant Judge has considered the evidence adduced by the respective parties and opined that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer in the disputed land. The relevant portion of the observations made by the trial Court is reproduced below: — 

 12. The pre-emptee in the written objection clearly stated that the case is barred by limitation. It is also contended that at the time of selling the property the seller opposite party No. 2 made a proposal to the pre-emptor for purchasing the said land but it was refused by him and, as such, the case is barred by estoppels, waiver and acquiescence. 

 16. I have also meticulously scrutinize the impugned judgment and order passed by the lower Appellate Court as well as the trial Court. On perusal of the impugned judgment and order it appears that to establish the matter of co-sharership the pre-emptor-appellant-opposite party did not adduce any evidence before the Additional District Judge but in allowing the Miscellaneous Appeal the learned Additional District Judge observed that the Pre-emptor is a co-sharer in the case land by way of inheritance. It further appears from the pre-emption petition that the pre-emptor has claimed pre-emption in respect of 192 decimals of land out of 62 decimals of land of CS Khatian No. 5, ROR Khatian No. 4 of Plot No. 37. In respect of co-sharership in the case land, PW 1 Shiplo Chandra Dhar in the cross-examination stated, “নাঃ খতিয়ানের জমি ৬২ ডিঃ এই খাতিয়ানে আমাদের জমি নাই। নিসত্তাবান হন......."
